native_result.query: Does increased time preference leads to higher BMI?
native_result.HypoA: Higher time preference associated with higher BMI for 1989 data.
native_result.WorkflowA:
1. Selected appropriate variables from the raw data
e.g.: Height: Height of respondent on 1985 instead of 1981.
      Income: Total net family income, 1989 (There are many other income variables in the raw data)
      Age:    Age of respondent at 1989 (Derived from Age at 1979).
Data Transformation:
2. Replaced -1 to -5 values (unavailable data) with NaN
3. Imputed the missing values in the AGE and INCOME variable with mean.
4. AGE_1989 had missing values, hence derived the variable as [AGE_1979 + 10]
5. Created a BMI variable using: bmi = (weight) * 0.453592 / (height) * 0.0254
6. Divided the Family income variable by 1000$ (Mentioned in the paper)
7. Created an AGE^2 variable (From the paper)
8. One-hot encoded RACE variable into BLACK and HISPANIC
9. One-hot encooded GENDER variable into MALE and FEMALE
10. Selected 'Was more money put into or taken out of R/spouse savings since last interview, 1989' as the Time Preference variable.
  DISSAVED = 1 if 'TOOK MORE MONEY OUT' else 0
  SAMESAVE = 1 if 'NO SAVINGS' or 'NO CHANGE' else 0
11. Dropped the unimportant columns for replication
12. DISSAVED and SAMESAVE as independent variables and BMI as dependent variable
13. Fit an OLS Regression Model
native_result.HypoB: In NLSY79, higher time preference (present-oriented financial behavior: dissaving, lower net savings flow, lower accumulated wealth) is associated with modestly higher BMI: dissavers in 1989 had ~0.26 BMI units higher BMI in 1989 (+0.45 vs savers when 'no savings' is modeled separately; 'no savings' group +0.54), each savings-flow quintile of higher saving is associated with -0.19 BMI units, and dissaving predicts BMI gain 1981-1989 (+0.20, p=0.028); obesity odds ratio 1.17 (p=0.058). Wealth accumulation 1985-1990 shows no association (p=0.71) while 1996 wealth level is weakly protective (-0.030, p=0.021). Contemporaneous income accounts for part of the association (coefficient attenuates to +0.17, p=0.23). The association is consistent in direction but modest (~0.2-0.5 BMI units); causality cannot be established from these observational data, and reverse causality is plausible.
native_result.WorkflowB: Validated 12,686x61 NLSY79 extract against schema; corrected units (weights lb->kg; Height 1981 decoded from feet-inches concatenation, Height 1985 used as adult height); recoded sentinels (weight 996, savings amounts >=1e6, grade 95, wealth/income top-codes); constructed BMI 1981/1989/1992 (plausible range 15-60); built time-preference exposures (dissaving indicator, 4-level savings direction with 'no savings' separate, winsorized/quintiled net savings flow, sign-log wealth growth 1985->1990, wealth level 1996); HC1-robust OLS of BMI 1989 and BMI change 1981->1989 and obesity logit adjusted for sex, race cohort, age, family size, parental and own education, ASVAB, log 1979 income, and an ever-institutionalized indicator; sensitivities: contemporaneous 1989 income (collider check), median+missing-indicator imputation of covariates, quintile exposures; complete-case n reported per spec (6,295 savings-direction; 3,481 net-flow; 5,244 wealth-growth; 4,245 wealth-1996) with covariate-balance/attrition diagnostics across specs.

sub_hypo.context: NLSY79 observational data; BMI restricted to 15–60. HC1-robust OLS adjusted for sex, racial/ethnic cohort, age, family size, parental and own education, ASVAB, log 1979 income, and ever-institutionalized status. Savings-direction complete-case n=6,295.

sub_hypo.relations: Dissavers have approximately 0.26 higher BMI units. With 'no savings' modeled separately, dissavers have 0.45 higher BMI units than savers, and the 'no savings' group has 0.54 higher BMI units. These are modest observational associations; causality is not established and reverse causality is plausible.
